newsitem.title: GERMANY: Initial German state CPI data shows tame inflation.
newsitem.headline: Initial German state CPI data shows tame inflation.

text.p: Two major German states on Tuesday reported a drop in consumer prices on a monthly basis in September, confirming economists' opinions that inflation was not a concern for the German economy.

The state of Baden-Wuerttemberg said consumer prices fell 0.2 percent month-on-month and were up 1.2 percent over year-ago levels while the state of North Rhine-Westphalia said prices fell 0.1 percent and were up 1.5 percent year-on-year.
The two states were the first of four states to release consumer price data for September, which will be used to compute provisional west German inflation for the month.
The states of Hesse and Bavaria are expected to release consumer price data in coming days and for west German data to be released on Thursday or Friday.
Economists said the reports were helped by seasonal adjustments but that inflation was not a concern.
"They look pretty favourable but the fact is that the numbers have benefitted for a strong seasonal effect," said Armin Kayser, economist at Swiss Bank Corp in Frankfurt.
"Consumer prices are currently bottoming out with no risk of acceleration but only a gradual upturn," he said.
Some economists said the modest pickup in year-on-year rates was due to an increase in energy prices, including a 17.7 percent gain in heating oil prices in Baden-Wuerttemberg.

Uwe Angenendt, economist at Berliner Handels und Frankfurter Bank, said: "I would see this as a temporary development and I do not think we will see any acceleration of inflation in the months to come," noting he expected an annual west German inflation rate of about 1.5 percent.
